title: John 4:27–42
context: The disciples return, startled that He talks with a woman, and stay silent. She leaves her jar, testifies in town, and people come. Jesus refuses their food: His food is the Father’s will. The fields are white; sower and reaper rejoice together. Many Samaritans believe because of her word, then many more because of His, and they confess Him Savior of the world.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: The harvest and the Savior of the world: older Arminian and Reformed writers, each in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: My meat is to do the will of him that sent me. Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields—the Samaritans who were coming. This is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world—not of the Jews only.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on John 4:34–35, 42)

reformed.quote: He calls it his food to do the will of the Father… The fields are already white: the Samaritans were coming in troops. They know that this is the Savior of the world. They had learned that the office of the Messiah is not confined to the Jews, but extends to the whole world.

verses.text: Just then, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why do you speak with her?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The disciples marvel, then keep silent. They still have a map of whom rabbis address. Grace is already ahead of their manners.

Disciples can be saved and still startled by Jesus’ company. The restraint from questioning is at least wisdom; the marvel shows how much they have to learn from the well.
verses.reformedNotes:
Just then: the timing keeps the disclosure (v. 26) between Jesus and the woman. Their marvel is social; their silence is mercy.

The Lord does not wait for His team’s comfort. He talks with whom He will, and they are not yet ready to interrogate it.

verses.text: So the woman left her water pot, went away into the city, and said to the people,
verses.arminianNotes:
The jar stays. The errand that brought her is outrun by the news. She goes to people, not away from them.

Imperfect theology can still run. Leaving the jar is a picture of a thirst reordered; speech to the town is already worship in truth beginning to overflow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Abandoned jar: narrative sermon. The well’s original purpose yields to witness.

The one who was sought (v. 23) becomes a seeker of her neighbors. Christ’s word creates a messenger before it finishes her catechism.

verses.text: “Come, see a man who told me everything that I have done. Can this be the Christ?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Come, see—echo of John’s Gospel invitations. She leads with being known, then a question, not a lecture: Can this be the Christ?

Honest wonder evangelizes. She does not claim to have solved Messiah; she invites inspection of the Man who told her her life. That is enough to start a town walking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Everything that I have done: the exposing word has become good news. Can this be—the question is open and loaded.

She repeats what He did, not a system. The Christ-question is the right one, and it is already His work in her mouth.

verses.text: They went out of the city, and were coming to him.
verses.arminianNotes:
They went, they were coming: a town in motion toward Jesus. Her question was not a dead end.

People can still come when invited. Fields white (v. 35) looks like this dusty road filling with Samaritans on the way to a tired Jew at a well.
verses.reformedNotes:
Outgoing and coming: John lets the harvest be visible before Jesus names it.

The Father-seeking of v. 23 now has a column of people. What she asked, they do; what He willed, they enact.

verses.text: In the meanwhile, the disciples urged him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Meanwhile, two kinds of hunger are at work. They urge lunch; He is mid-harvest.

Care for Jesus’ body is not wrong, and still can miss His work. Disciples will need their eyes lifted from bread to fields.
verses.reformedNotes:
Rabbi, eat: ordinary love, small horizon.

They went to buy food (v. 8) and return to feed a Lord whose food is elsewhere. The lesson is about to be the Father’s will.

verses.text: But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Unknown food: they will mishear it as a secret snack, as she misheard living water.

Jesus keeps offering a different nourishment than His people first imagine. Knowing this food is part of learning Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Food they do not know: knowledge gap again, as in 4:10.

The Son’s sustenance is hidden from even close disciples until He speaks it. Union with the Father’s will is His meal.

verses.text: The disciples therefore said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”
verses.arminianNotes:
They confer horizontally and stay in the cupboard. The woman is bringing a town; they are checking catering.

John is not cruel to them. Literalism is the Gospel’s running joke because grace keeps translating it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Has anyone brought: they cannot yet hear “food” as vocation.

Even the Twelve need the well’s lesson. Knowing Christ includes knowing what feeds Him.

verses.text: Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.
verses.arminianNotes:
Food = the Sender’s will done and finished. The well conversation was not a delay of lunch; it was lunch.

Jesus’ satisfaction is the accomplished work of the Father. Disciples are invited into that appetite—doing sent-will, not merely admiring it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: He calls it his food to do the Father’s will. Sent and accomplish: mission with a completion.

The Sender’s will is the Son’s life. Harvest in Samaria is not extra credit; it is the work given Him to finish.

verses.text: Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest’? Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.
verses.arminianNotes:
Proverbial delay versus present white fields. Lift up your eyes—Wesley saw the Samaritans coming. The harvest is not later; it is walking toward them.

Waiting four months is disobedience when the field is already pale. The gospel’s whoever is showing up in time; eyes must be lifted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Four months is farm-sense; white now is kingdom-sense. Look, I tell you.

The hour that is now (v. 23) has a visible crop. God has ripened a people the disciples did not plant this morning.

verses.text: He who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit to eternal life, that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.
verses.arminianNotes:
Already: wages and eternal fruit now. Sower and reaper share one joy, not a rivalry of credits.

Some speak, some gather, God gives the life. Rejoicing together is the Baptist’s joy (3:29) extended to a whole crew.
verses.reformedNotes:
Wages already, fruit for eternal life, joint joy. The economy is God’s.

Eternal life as crop means this is not mere enthusiasm. The Father pays and gathers; human roles are assigned so they can be glad together.

verses.text: For in this the saying is true, ‘One sows, and another reaps.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Division of labor without division of church. Here the proverb is gospel: you may reap what you did not start.

Today’s convert may be yesterday’s unknown sowing. Grace lets us enter others’ labor without pretending we were first.
verses.reformedNotes:
The saying holds here: God chains servants across time.

Sowing and reaping are distinct gifts (as in 1 Cor 3). No reaper may boast as if the field began with his sickle.

verses.text: I sent you to reap that for which you haven’t labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”
verses.arminianNotes:
I sent you: their reaping is assignment, not luck. Others—prophets, Baptist, the woman minutes ago—labored first.

Being sent to reap is gift and task. Entering others’ labor means the Samaritans’ faith will not be a disciples’ trophy.
verses.reformedNotes:
I sent: the Son is the sender of reapers into a field others worked.

They reap a harvest they did not earn. They enter labor God has already been doing through others, including this noon’s witness.

verses.text: From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything that I have done.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Many believed because of her testimony. A five-husband history became the sentence God used.

God uses told-truth about a life. Belief can begin on a neighbor’s word; v. 42 will deepen it without despising this beginning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Because of the woman’s testimony: means of faith named. Many, not all, believed.

The Spirit can hitch saving faith to a short, true story. The content is still Him—He told me—not her pedigree.

verses.text: So when the Samaritans came to him, they begged him to stay with them. He stayed there two days.
verses.arminianNotes:
They ask Him to stay; He stays two days. The One who “had to” pass through now has to linger because they want Him.

Remaining is mercy. Two days of the Word in a Samaritan town is the love of 3:16 with a guest-room.
verses.reformedNotes:
Asked, and He stayed. The necessity of v. 4 blossoms into two days of presence.

The Word tabernacles where He is asked, and the asking itself is fruit of the work He already did at the well.

verses.text: Many more believed because of his word.
verses.arminianNotes:
Her testimony opened; His word confirmed and increased.

Hearing Christ Himself is better, and the first hearing was not fake. Faith grows as the object of faith speaks.
verses.reformedNotes:
His word is the higher cause of more faith. The increase is attributed to what He said.

The Son’s speech creates believers. Two days of word explain “many more” better than two days of atmosphere.

verses.text: They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Not ungrateful to her: they have now heard for themselves. Savior of the world—Wesley: not of the Jews only. Samaria names the wide title first in this Gospel’s narrative.

Arminian interpreters receive this confession as the point of 3:16 on the ground. World is not a hint; it is the town’s conclusion after hearing Him. The Savior is for more than one mountain’s people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: they learned Messiah’s office extends to the whole world. Heard for ourselves, we know: faith’s certainty after the Word.

Savior of the world is John’s high title, and it does not undo 3:3–8 or 3:27. The One who saves the world does so as people hear and believe; Samaria is proof the field was never only Judea.
verses.keyContrast: Both readings hold: they know Jesus as Savior of the world by hearing Him, not by remaining under secondhand report. Arminians take the title as sincere universal saving intent now arriving in Samaria. Calvin’s heirs generally take it as Messiah’s worldwide office—nations included—without treating “world” as a guarantee that every person will believe.
